title: Ἕκτωρ καὶ ἄλοχος
about: Paris answers Hector’s rebuke: it was grief, not anger, that kept him in the chamber, his wife has talked him into the war, and he will follow once he has armed. Hector says nothing to him, but Helen speaks, calling herself a dog and wishing a storm-blast had swept her away on the day she was born; she asks Hector to sit down, since the toil of the war has fallen on him for her sake and Paris’. Hector refuses: his heart is set on defending the Trojans, and she is to rouse Paris to catch him up inside the city. He means first to see his household, not knowing whether he will come back. At home he does not find Andromache; the housekeeper tells him she has hurried to the tower and the wall, like a woman out of her mind, with the nurse carrying the child. He goes back through the streets and meets her at the Scaean Gates, with her son in a handmaid’s arms. He smiles at the boy in silence. Andromache takes his hand and begs him to pity them: his strength will kill him, Achilles killed her father and her seven brothers and ransomed her mother, who then died, and Hector is all she has. She asks him to stay on the tower and to post the army by the wild fig-tree, where the wall can most easily be attacked and where, she says, the best men have three times tried it.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Alexander godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: Then Alexander, godlike in form, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Paris now answers the rebuke Hector made at the end of the last part; Ἀλέξανδρος ‘Alexander’ is Paris’ other name. τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ‘and him in turn he addressed’ uses the long epic form of the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’, and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the reply. θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ is his stock epithet.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἐπεί με κατ’ αἶσαν ἐνείκεσας οὐδ’ ὑπὲρ αἶσαν,
τοὔνεκά τοι ἐρέω·
sentences.l:
“Hector, since me in due measure you reviled and not beyond due measure,
for that reason I will tell you;
sentences.i: “Hector, since you have reviled me in due measure, and not beyond it, that is why I will tell you;
sentences.n: Paris admits that Hector’s rebuke was fair. ἐνείκεσας is the aorist of νεικέω ‘reproach, revile’, and κατ’ αἶσαν ‘according to due measure’ is set against ὑπὲρ αἶσαν ‘beyond due measure’: the reproach was just, not excessive. τοὔνεκά (= τοῦ ἕνεκα) ‘for that reason’ answers ἐπεί ‘since’, τοι is ‘to you’, and ἐρέω is the future ‘I will tell’. Hector’s name stands first as a vocative.

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ σύνθεο καί μευ ἄκουσον·
sentences.l: and you, take it in, and hear me:
sentences.i: and you must take it in and hear me:
sentences.n: σὺ δὲ ‘and you’ sets Hector’s part, listening, against Paris’, telling. σύνθεο is the aorist imperative middle of συντίθημι, literally ‘put together’, and here means ‘take it in, grasp it’. μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, the case ἀκούω takes for the person heard, and ἄκουσον is its aorist imperative.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοι ἐγὼ Τρώων τόσσον χόλῳ οὐδὲ νεμέσσι
ἥμην ἐν θαλάμῳ, ἔθελον δ’ ἄχεϊ προτραπέσθαι.
sentences.l:
Not, I tell you, so much in anger at the Trojans nor in resentment
was I sitting in the chamber, but I wished to give myself over to grief.
sentences.i: It was not so much in anger at the Trojans, or in resentment, that I sat in my chamber; I wanted to give myself over to grief.
sentences.n: Paris explains why he stayed out of the fighting: grief, not anger. οὔ τοι is ‘not, I tell you’ (τοι a particle of assertion), and τόσσον ‘so much’ goes with both datives, χόλῳ ‘in anger’ and νεμέσσι ‘in resentment’, the second the dative of νέμεσις spelled with doubled σ; Τρώων ‘at the Trojans’ is taken with both. ἥμην is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’, ἄχεϊ the dative of ἄχος ‘grief’, and προτραπέσθαι the aorist infinitive of προτρέπομαι ‘turn oneself to’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ με παρειποῦσ’ ἄλοχος μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσιν
ὅρμησ’ ἐς πόλεμον·
sentences.l:
But now my wife, talking me round with soft words,
urged me on into the war;
sentences.i: But now my wife has talked me round with soft words and urged me into the war;
sentences.n: Paris names his wife as the one who sent him back to the fighting. παρειποῦσ’ is the aorist participle of παρεῖπον ‘talk round, win over’, with the dative μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσιν ‘soft words’ (-εσσιν is the epic dative plural). ἄλοχος ‘wife’ is Helen. ὅρμησ’ is ὥρμησε without its augment, the aorist of ὁρμάω used of setting someone in motion, ‘urged on’.

sentences.t:
δοκέει δέ μοι ὧδε καὶ αὐτῷ
λώϊον ἔσσεσθαι·
sentences.l:
and it seems to me thus, to myself as well,
that it will be better;
sentences.i: and it seems to me myself, too, that it will be better so;
sentences.n: Paris adds his own opinion to Helen’s. δοκέει is the uncontracted δοκεῖ ‘it seems’, and μοι … καὶ αὐτῷ ‘to me myself as well’ joins his view to hers. ὧδε ‘thus, in this way’ stands between the two verbs and could go with either; the literal English leaves it beside ‘seems’, and the idiomatic English takes it with ‘better’. λώϊον is the neuter comparative ‘better’, and ἔσσεσθαι the future infinitive of εἰμί with doubled σ, ‘will be’.

sentences.t: νίκη δ’ ἐπαμείβεται ἄνδρας.
sentences.l: and victory goes in turn over men.
sentences.i: for victory passes from one man to another.
sentences.n: A general saying, offered in support of going back to the fight. νίκη ‘victory’ is the subject; ἐπαμείβεται is the middle of ἐπαμείβω ‘exchange’, here ‘go by turns’, and ἄνδρας is the accusative of the men it passes over. The sense is that victory does not stay with one side.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἐπίμεινον, Ἀρήϊα τεύχεα δύω·
sentences.l: But come now, wait, while I put on warlike armour;
sentences.i: But come now, wait while I put on my warlike armour;
sentences.n: Paris asks Hector to wait while he arms. ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ‘but come now’; ἐπίμεινον is the aorist imperative of ἐπιμένω ‘wait’. Ἀρήϊα ‘warlike’ is the adjective from Ἄρης, and τεύχεα is ‘armour’. δύω ‘I put on’ is in sense a subjunctive after the command, ‘while I put on’.

sentences.t: ἢ ἴθ’, ἐγὼ δὲ μέτειμι·
sentences.l: or go, and I will follow after;
sentences.i: or else go, and I will come after you;
sentences.n: Paris leaves the choice to Hector. ἢ ‘or’; ἴθ’ is ἴθι, the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἐγὼ δὲ ‘and I’ answers it. μέτειμι is μετά + εἶμι ‘I will go after, follow’, not a form of ‘be among’; the present has a future sense.

sentences.t: κιχήσεσθαι δέ σ’ ὀΐω.
sentences.l: and I suspect that I shall overtake you.”
sentences.i: and I suspect that I shall catch up with you.”
sentences.n: ὀΐω ‘I suspect’ takes the infinitive κιχήσεσθαι, the future middle of κιχάνω ‘reach, overtake’, with σ’ (σε) as its object; δέ ‘and’ joins it to the offer to follow. Paris’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and him not at all addressed Hector of the glancing helmet;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector of the glancing helmet said nothing at all to him;
sentences.n: Hector does not answer Paris; Helen speaks next. ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ ends Paris’ speech, and τὸν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη ‘and him not at all did he address’ uses προσέφη, the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is Hector’s stock epithet (κόρυς ‘helmet’ + αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’).

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἑλένη μύθοισι προσηύδα μειλιχίοισι·
sentences.l: Him then Helen addressed with gentle words:
sentences.i: Then Helen spoke to him with gentle words:
sentences.n: Helen speaks to Hector, who has just said nothing to Paris. μύθοισι is the dative plural of μῦθος ‘word’ and μειλιχίοισι ‘gentle’ agrees with it. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’, and τὸν ‘him’ is Hector.

sentences.t: δᾶερ ἐμεῖο κυνὸς κακομηχάνου ὀκρυοέσσης,
sentences.l: “Husband’s-brother of me, a dog, evil-contriving, chilling,
sentences.i: “My husband’s brother, and so kin to a dog like me, a contriver of evil, a chilling thing,
sentences.n: Helen opens by calling herself a dog. δᾶερ is the vocative of δαήρ ‘husband’s brother’: Hector is Paris’ brother, so her husband’s brother. The genitive ἐμεῖο ‘of me’ (epic for ἐμοῦ) depends on it, and κυνός ‘of a dog’ is added to ἐμεῖο, so that she is the ‘dog’; κύων is a word of abuse, shameless creature. κακομηχάνου ‘contriving evil’ and ὀκρυοέσσης (the rare ὀκρυόεις, traditionally ‘chilling’) also go with κυνός, and so with ἐμεῖο, and the feminine ending of ὀκρυοέσσης shows she is speaking of herself.

sentences.t:
ὥς μ’ ὄφελ’ ἤματι τῷ ὅτε με πρῶτον τέκε μήτηρ
οἴχεσθαι προφέρουσα κακὴ ἀνέμοιο θύελλα
εἰς ὄρος ἢ εἰς κῦμα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης,
ἔνθά με κῦμ’ ἀπόερσε πάρος τάδε ἔργα γενέσθαι.
sentences.l:
Would that, on the day when first my mother bore me,
an evil storm-blast had gone off bearing me forth
to a mountain or to a wave of the much-roaring sea,
where the wave swept me away before these deeds came to be,
sentences.i: If only, on the day my mother first bore me, an evil storm-blast had carried me off to a mountain or to a wave of the loud-roaring sea, where the wave would have swept me away before these deeds came to be,
sentences.n: A wish that she had died at birth. ὥς … ὄφελ’ with an infinitive is a wish, ‘would that’, here about the past that cannot be undone: ὄφελ’ is ὄφελε, from ὀφείλω ‘ought’, and the infinitive is οἴχεσθαι ‘to have gone’, with προφέρουσα ‘carrying forth’ and the subject κακὴ ἀνέμοιο θύελλα ‘an evil storm-blast of wind’. ἤματι τῷ ὅτε ‘on the day when’. ἔνθά ‘where’ begins a clause saying what would then have happened: ἀπόερσε is a rare aorist ‘swept away’, and πάρος … γενέσθαι is ‘before … came to be’. πολυφλοίσβοιο ‘loud-roaring’ is the stock epithet of the sea.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τάδε γ’ ὧδε θεοὶ κακὰ τεκμήραντο,
ἀνδρὸς ἔπειτ’ ὤφελλον ἀμείνονος εἶναι ἄκοιτις,
ὃς ᾔδη νέμεσίν τε καὶ αἴσχεα πόλλ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l:
But since the gods fixed these evils in this way,
then would that I were wife of a better man,
who knew resentment and the many shames of men.
sentences.i: But since the gods have fixed these evils in this way, then if only I had been the wife of a better man, one who knew men’s resentment and their many shames.
sentences.n: Helen’s second wish: since the evil cannot be undone, that she were at least married to a better man. ἐπεί … τεκμήραντο is ‘since the gods fixed’, τεκμαίρομαι ‘fix, ordain’ with κακά ‘evils’ as object; τάδε γ’ ὧδε is ‘these things at least, in this way’. ὤφελλον with the infinitive εἶναι is a wish again, with ἄκοιτις ‘wife’ and the genitive ἀνδρὸς … ἀμείνονος ‘of a better man’. ᾔδη (= ᾔδει) is the old past of οἶδα, ‘knew’, and its objects are νέμεσιν ‘resentment’ and αἴσχεα, the plural of αἶσχος ‘shame, disgrace’.

sentences.t:
τούτῳ δ’ οὔτ’ ἂρ νῦν φρένες ἔμπεδοι οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ὀπίσσω
ἔσσονται·
sentences.l:
But for this man neither now are the wits firm, nor in time to come
will they be;
sentences.i: But this man’s wits are not firm now, and will not be in time to come;
sentences.n: Helen turns to Paris, and says he cannot be relied on. τούτῳ δ’ ‘but to this man’, Paris, is a dative of possession with φρένες ἔμπεδοι ‘firm wits’; οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, with νῦν ‘now’ and ὀπίσσω ‘in time to come’. ἔσσονται is ἔσονται, the future of εἰμί with doubled σ, and stands first in the next line.

sentences.t: τὼ καί μιν ἐπαυρήσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.l: therefore I suspect that he too will have the benefit of it.
sentences.i: and so I suspect that he, too, will have the benefit of it.
sentences.n: Helen predicts a bitter result for Paris. τὼ is τῷ ‘therefore’; μιν ‘him’ is Paris, with καί ‘too’. ἐπαυρήσεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἐπαυρίσκομαι ‘have the benefit of’, which is neutral in sense and bitter in tone here: he will get what his unsteady wits bring. The Greek gives no object; ‘of it’ is supplied. ὀΐω ‘I suspect’ governs the infinitive.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν εἴσελθε καὶ ἕζεο τῷδ’ ἐπὶ δίφρῳ
δᾶερ,
sentences.l:
But come now, come in and sit on this stool,
husband’s-brother,
sentences.i: But come now, come in and sit on this stool, my husband’s brother,
sentences.n: Helen invites Hector in. ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ‘but come now’; εἴσελθε is the aorist imperative of εἰσέρχομαι ‘come in’, and ἕζεο the imperative of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’. δίφρος here is a seat, ‘stool’ (the same word can also mean ‘chariot’), and τῷδ’ ‘this’ points to it. δᾶερ is the vocative ‘husband’s brother’ again.

sentences.t:
ἐπεί σε μάλιστα πόνος φρένας ἀμφιβέβηκεν
εἵνεκ’ ἐμεῖο κυνὸς καὶ Ἀλεξάνδρου ἕνεκ’ ἄτης,
οἷσιν ἐπὶ Ζεὺς θῆκε κακὸν μόρον, ὡς καὶ ὀπίσσω
ἀνθρώποισι πελώμεθ’ ἀοίδιμοι ἐσσομένοισι.
sentences.l:
since toil most of all has come around your wits
because of me, a dog, and because of Alexander’s bewilderment,
upon whom Zeus set an evil doom, that even hereafter
we may be sung-of for men yet to come.”
sentences.i: since toil has come around your wits most of all, because of me, a dog, and because of Alexander’s bewilderment; Zeus has set an evil doom on the two of us, so that even in time to come we may be a subject of song for men yet to be born.”
sentences.n: Helen gives her reason for the invitation. ἐπεί σε … πόνος φρένας ἀμφιβέβηκεν is ‘since toil has come around your wits’: ἀμφιβέβηκεν is the perfect of ἀμφιβαίνω ‘go round, encompass’, with σε and φρένας both accusative, ‘you, in your wits’. εἵνεκ’ (= ἕνεκα) ‘because of’ is used twice, with ἐμεῖο κυνός ‘me, a dog’ and Ἀλεξάνδρου … ἄτης ‘Alexander’s bewilderment’. οἷσιν ‘upon whom’ is a relative plural for the two of them; ἐπὶ … θῆκε is ‘set upon’, and μόρον is ‘doom’. ὡς with the subjunctive πελώμεθ’ (πέλομαι ‘be’) gives purpose, and ἀοίδιμοι means ‘sung of, a subject of song’. Helen’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: Her then answered great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then great Hector of the glancing helmet answered her:
sentences.n: Hector answers Helen. τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘and then he answered her’ is the usual reply-line: ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and τὴν ‘her’ is Helen. μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ ‘great Hector of the glancing helmet’ names him in full.

sentences.t: μή με κάθιζ’ Ἑλένη φιλέουσά περ·
sentences.l: “Do not seat me, Helen, loving me though you do;
sentences.i: “Do not make me sit down, Helen, though you love me;
sentences.n: Hector refuses Helen’s invitation. μή with the present imperative κάθιζ’ (καθίζω, here transitive ‘make sit, seat’) is ‘do not seat me’; Ἑλένη is the vocative. φιλέουσά περ ‘though you love me’ has the concessive περ, and φιλέω ‘love’ includes friendly treatment: she means well, and he still refuses.

sentences.t: οὐδέ με πείσεις·
sentences.l: and you will not persuade me;
sentences.i: and you will not persuade me;
sentences.n: οὐδέ ‘and … not’ makes a second refusal. πείσεις is the future of πείθω ‘persuade’, with με ‘me’ as object. The next lines give his reasons.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ μοι θυμὸς ἐπέσσυται ὄφρ’ ἐπαμύνω
Τρώεσσ’, οἳ μέγ’ ἐμεῖο ποθὴν ἀπεόντος ἔχουσιν.
sentences.l:
For already my heart is rushing on, so that I may come to the defence of
the Trojans, who greatly feel the lack of me while I am away.
sentences.i: For my heart is already rushing on, so that I may come to the defence of the Trojans, who greatly feel the lack of me while I am away.
sentences.n: Hector’s first reason: the Trojans need him. θυμὸς ἐπέσσυται ‘my heart is rushing on’ (ἐπέσσυται, the perfect of ἐπισεύω, with μοι ‘in me’); ὄφρ’ ἐπαμύνω is a purpose clause, ‘so that I may come to the defence of’, with the dative Τρώεσσ’. ποθή is ‘lack, longing’ and ἔχουσιν ‘they have’ it, so ‘they feel the lack of me’; ἀπεόντος (= ἀπόντος) agrees with ἐμεῖο, ‘me, being away’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ ὄρνυθι τοῦτον, ἐπειγέσθω δὲ καὶ αὐτός,
ὥς κεν ἔμ’ ἔντοσθεν πόλιος καταμάρψῃ ἐόντα.
sentences.l:
But you, rouse this man, and let him hurry himself too,
so that he may overtake me, being inside the city.
sentences.i: But you, rouse him, and let him hurry too, so that he overtakes me while I am inside the city.
sentences.n: Hector tells Helen to urge Paris on. ὄρνυθι is the imperative of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, with τοῦτον ‘this man’ for Paris; ἐπειγέσθω ‘let him hurry himself’ is a third-person imperative, and καὶ αὐτός ‘himself too’. ὥς κεν … καταμάρψῃ is a purpose clause, ‘so that he may overtake’ (καταμάρπτω), ἔμ’ ἐόντα ‘me being’ ἔντοσθεν πόλιος ‘inside the city’: Paris is to catch him before he has left the town.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼν οἶκον δὲ ἐλεύσομαι ὄφρα ἴδωμαι
οἰκῆας ἄλοχόν τε φίλην καὶ νήπιον υἱόν.
sentences.l:
For indeed I myself will go homewards, so that I may see
the household servants, and my dear wife, and my infant son.
sentences.i: For I will go home to see my household servants, my dear wife, and my little son.
sentences.n: Hector says where he goes first: home. καὶ γάρ ‘for indeed’; ἐγὼν is ἐγώ with a final ν; οἶκον δέ is printed as two words and means ‘homewards’ (-δε marks direction); ἐλεύσομαι is the future of ἔρχομαι. ὄφρα ἴδωμαι ‘so that I may see’ is a purpose clause. οἰκῆας are the members of the household, servants; ἄλοχον ‘wife’ and νήπιον υἱόν ‘infant son’ complete the list.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ οἶδ’ εἰ ἔτι σφιν ὑπότροπος ἵξομαι αὖτις,
ἦ ἤδη μ’ ὑπὸ χερσὶ θεοὶ δαμόωσιν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
For I do not know whether I shall yet come back to them again,
or whether already the gods will subdue me beneath the hands of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: For I do not know whether I shall come back to them again, or whether the gods will already overcome me at the hands of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: Hector gives his second reason: he may not come back. οὐ γὰρ οἶδ’ εἰ … ἦ is ‘for I do not know whether … or whether’; ὑπότροπος ‘returning’ describes him, ἵξομαι is the future of ἱκνέομαι ‘I shall come’, and ἔτι σφιν … αὖτις is ‘yet again to them’. δαμόωσιν is a subjunctive of δαμάω (= δαμάζω) ‘subdue, overcome’, with ὑπὸ χερσὶ … Ἀχαιῶν ‘beneath the hands of the Achaeans’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: So then, having spoken, went away Hector of the glancing helmet;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Hector of the glancing helmet went off;
sentences.n: Hector’s speech is over and he leaves. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ‘so then, having spoken’ is the usual closing line, with φωνήσας ‘having lifted his voice’; ἀπέβη is the aorist of ἀποβαίνω ‘go away’. The scene moves from Paris’ house to Hector’s own.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἔπειθ’ ἵκανε δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας,
οὐδ’ εὗρ’ Ἀνδρομάχην λευκώλενον ἐν μεγάροισιν,
ἀλλ’ ἥ γε ξὺν παιδὶ καὶ ἀμφιπόλῳ ἐϋπέπλῳ
πύργῳ ἐφεστήκει γοόωσά τε μυρομένη τε.
sentences.l:
And quickly then he came to the well-inhabited house,
and did not find white-armed Andromache in the halls,
but she, with her child and a fair-robed handmaid,
was standing on the tower, sobbing and mourning.
sentences.i: He quickly came to his well-inhabited house, and did not find white-armed Andromache in the halls; she, with her child and a fair-robed handmaid, was standing on the tower, sobbing and mourning.
sentences.n: Hector finds the house without its mistress. αἶψα ‘quickly’; ἵκανε is the imperfect of ἱκάνω ‘come to’; δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας ‘the well-inhabited house’ (the plural δόμοι stands for one house). εὗρ’ is the aorist of εὑρίσκω with its ending elided. ἥ γε ‘she’ uses the article as a pronoun. ἐφεστήκει is the pluperfect of ἐφίστημι with the sense ‘was standing upon’, and πύργῳ is the dative of place. γοόωσα and μυρομένη are participles, ‘sobbing’ and ‘mourning’; ἐϋπέπλῳ ‘fair-robed’ and λευκώλενον ‘white-armed’ are stock epithets.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὡς οὐκ ἔνδον ἀμύμονα τέτμεν ἄκοιτιν
ἔστη ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰών, μετὰ δὲ δμῳῇσιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
And Hector, when he did not come upon the blameless wife within,
stood at the threshold, as he went, and among the maidservants spoke:
sentences.i: When Hector did not find his blameless wife within, he came to a stand on the threshold and spoke among the maids:
sentences.n: Hector, not finding her, questions the maids. ὡς here is ‘when’; οὐκ ἔνδον ‘not within’; τέτμεν is an old aorist ‘came upon, found’; ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose sense is not known, and the translation keeps ‘blameless’ every time. ἔστη ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰών ‘came to a stand on the threshold, going’; μετὰ … ἔειπεν ‘spoke among’ is one verb split in two, with δμῳῇσιν the dative plural of δμῳή ‘maidservant’.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἄγε μοι δμῳαὶ νημερτέα μυθήσασθε·
sentences.l: “But come, tell me unerring things, maidservants:
sentences.i: “Come now, maids, tell me unerring things:
sentences.n: Hector’s demand opens his questions. εἰ δ’ ἄγε is an urging idiom, ‘come now’ (εἰ is part of it, not ‘if’); μοι ‘to me’; δμῳαί is the vocative ‘maidservants’. νημερτέα, the neuter plural of νημερτής ‘unerring’, is the object of μυθήσασθε, the aorist imperative middle of μυθέομαι ‘tell’.

sentences.t: πῇ ἔβη Ἀνδρομάχη λευκώλενος ἐκ μεγάροιο;
sentences.l: Where did Andromache, white-armed, go from the hall?
sentences.i: Where has white-armed Andromache gone out of the hall?
sentences.n: πῇ ‘where’; ἔβη is the aorist of βαίνω ‘went’. ἐκ μεγάροιο ‘out of the hall’ has the singular and the epic genitive -οιο. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is Andromache’s stock epithet. Hector asks first, and the next lines add three guesses.

sentences.l:
Or anywhere to her husband’s sisters or to the fair-robed wives of her husband’s brothers
or to Athena’s has she gone out, where the other
fine-plaited Trojan women appease the dread goddess?”
sentences.i: Or has she gone out anywhere to my sisters, or to my brothers’ fair-robed wives, or to Athena’s temple, where the other fine-plaited Trojan women appease the dread goddess?”
sentences.n: Hector offers three places Andromache might be. ἠέ πῃ ‘or anywhere’; γαλόων is the genitive plural of γάλως ‘husband’s sister’ and εἰνατέρων the genitive plural of εἰνάτηρ ‘wife of a husband’s brother’, both named from Andromache’s side, so they are Hector’s own sisters and his brothers’ wives. The Greek leaves out the word ‘house’ after them and ‘temple’ after Ἀθηναίης ‘Athena’s’. ἐξοίχεται ‘has gone out’ serves for all three. ἔνθά περ ‘just where’; ἐϋπλόκαμοι ‘fine-plaited’ and ἐϋπέπλων ‘fair-robed’ are stock epithets of women; ἱλάσκονται ‘they appease’, with δεινὴν θεόν ‘the dread goddess’, Athena. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ ὀτρηρὴ ταμίη πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: Him then in turn the brisk housekeeper addressed with a word:
sentences.i: Then the brisk housekeeper spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The housekeeper replies. τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ ‘and him in turn’; ὀτρηρή ‘brisk’ is her epithet, and ταμίη is the feminine of ταμίης ‘steward’, so ‘housekeeper’. πρὸς … ἔειπεν is one verb split in two (= προσεῖπεν) ‘addressed’, with μῦθον ‘a word’ as its object.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἐπεὶ μάλ’ ἄνωγας ἀληθέα μυθήσασθαι,
οὔτέ πῃ ἐς γαλόων οὔτ’ εἰνατέρων ἐϋπέπλων
οὔτ’ ἐς Ἀθηναίης ἐξοίχεται, ἔνθά περ ἄλλαι
Τρῳαὶ ἐϋπλόκαμοι δεινὴν θεὸν ἱλάσκονται,
sentences.l:
“Hector, since you so strongly bid me tell true things,
neither anywhere to her husband’s sisters nor to the fair-robed wives of her husband’s brothers
nor to Athena’s has she gone out, where the other
fine-plaited Trojan women appease the dread goddess,
sentences.i: “Hector, since you press me so to tell the truth, she has gone out neither to your sisters, nor to your brothers’ fair-robed wives, nor to Athena’s temple, where the other fine-plaited Trojan women appease the dread goddess,
sentences.n: The housekeeper answers Hector’s three guesses with three denials. ἐπεὶ μάλ’ ἄνωγας ἀληθέα μυθήσασθαι ‘since you so strongly bid me tell true things’: ἄνωγας ‘you bid’, ἀληθέα neuter plural ‘true things’. The next three lines echo his question, with οὔτε … οὔτε … οὔτ’ ‘neither … nor … nor’ in place of his ‘or … or’; the kinship words are the same, still named from Andromache’s side, so here they are ‘your sisters’ and ‘your brothers’ wives’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πύργον ἔβη μέγαν Ἰλίου, οὕνεκ’ ἄκουσε
τείρεσθαι Τρῶας, μέγα δὲ κράτος εἶναι Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
but she went to the great tower of Ilios, because she heard
that the Trojans are being worn down, and that the strength of the Achaeans is great.
sentences.i: but she has gone to the great tower of Ilios, because she heard that the Trojans are being worn down and that the Achaeans’ strength is great.
sentences.n: She says where Andromache has gone, and why. ἐπὶ πύργον … μέγαν Ἰλίου ‘to the great tower of Ilios’, with μέγαν ‘great’ after the verb; οὕνεκ’ (= οὗ ἕνεκα) ‘because’ introduces what she heard, in infinitives: τείρεσθαι ‘to be worn down’ (passive of τείρω) and εἶναι ‘to be’, with μέγα κράτος ‘great strength’ (κράτος here includes the sense of mastery in the fighting).

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν δὴ πρὸς τεῖχος ἐπειγομένη ἀφικάνει
μαινομένῃ ἐϊκυῖα·
sentences.l:
She indeed, hurrying, arrives at the wall,
like to one raging;
sentences.i: Hurrying to the wall, she arrives like a woman out of her mind;
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν δή ‘she, indeed’; ἐπειγομένη ‘hurrying’; ἀφικάνει is the present of ἀφικάνω (= ἀφικνέομαι) ‘arrive’, in a report of what is happening now. μαινομένῃ ἐϊκυῖα ‘like one raging’: ἐϊκυῖα is the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, which takes the dative, and μαίνομαι means ‘rage, be frantic’; ‘a woman out of her mind’ gives the sense.

sentences.t: φέρει δ’ ἅμα παῖδα τιθήνη.
sentences.l: and along with her carries the child the nurse.”
sentences.i: and the nurse is carrying the child along with her.”
sentences.n: τιθήνη ‘nurse’ is the woman who tends the child; φέρει ‘carries’ and ἅμα ‘along with her’ make the baby part of what the housekeeper reports. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα γυνὴ ταμίη, ὃ δ’ ἀπέσσυτο δώματος Ἕκτωρ
τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδὸν αὖτις ἐϋκτιμένας κατ’ ἀγυιάς.
sentences.l:
She spoke, the woman, the housekeeper, and he rushed away from the house, Hector,
the same way again through the well-built streets.
sentences.i: So the housekeeper spoke, and Hector rushed out of the house, back by the same road through the well-built streets.
sentences.n: The housekeeper has finished and Hector hurries back. ἦ ῥα ‘she spoke’ (ἦ is an old past of ‘say’), with the subject γυνὴ ταμίη ‘the woman, the housekeeper’ added. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’; ἀπέσσυτο is the aorist of ἀποσεύομαι ‘rush away’, and δώματος is the genitive of the place left. τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδὸν αὖτις ‘the same way again’; ἐϋκτιμένας ‘well-built’ goes with ἀγυιάς ‘streets’, and κατά is ‘through’.

sentences.t:
εὖτε πύλας ἵκανε διερχόμενος μέγα ἄστυ
Σκαιάς, τῇ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε διεξίμεναι πεδίον δέ,
sentences.l:
When to the gates he came, passing through the great town,
the Scaean Gates, by which he was about to go out to the plain,
sentences.i: When he came to the Scaean Gates, passing through the great town, by which he was about to go out to the plain,
sentences.n: Hector reaches the Scaean Gates. εὖτε ‘when’; πύλας … Σκαιάς ‘the Scaean Gates’, with Σκαιάς at the start of the second line; διερχόμενος ‘passing through’ takes μέγα ἄστυ ‘the great town’ as its object. τῇ ‘by which’; ἔμελλε διεξίμεναι ‘was about to go out through’, the infinitive of διέξειμι; πεδίον δέ ‘to the plain’ (the -δε of direction, printed apart).

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλοχος πολύδωρος ἐναντίη ἦλθε θέουσα
Ἀνδρομάχη θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἠετίωνος
Ἠετίων ὃς ἔναιεν ὑπὸ Πλάκῳ ὑληέσσῃ
Θήβῃ Ὑποπλακίῃ Κιλίκεσσ’ ἄνδρεσσιν ἀνάσσων·
sentences.l:
There his wife, rich in gifts, came running to meet him,
Andromache, daughter of great-spirited Eetion,
Eetion, who dwelt beneath wooded Placus,
in Hypoplacian Thebe, ruling over Cilician men;
sentences.i: There his wife, rich in gifts, came running to meet him: Andromache, daughter of great-spirited Eetion, Eetion who dwelt beneath wooded Placus in Hypoplacian Thebe, and was lord over the Cilician men;
sentences.n: Andromache runs to meet him, and her father is named. ἔνθ’ ‘there’; ἄλοχος ‘wife’; πολύδωρος ‘rich in gifts’ (the Greek does not say whether she brought many or many were given for her); ἐναντίη ‘opposite, to meet him’; ἦλθε θέουσα ‘came running’. θυγάτηρ μεγαλήτορος Ἠετίωνος ‘daughter of great-spirited Eetion’ is followed by a relative clause on Eetion himself: ὃς ἔναιεν ‘who dwelt’; ὑπὸ Πλάκῳ ὑληέσσῃ ‘beneath wooded Placus’ (a wooded height); Θήβῃ Ὑποπλακίῃ ‘in Hypoplacian Thebe’, the second word meaning ‘under Placus’; Κιλίκεσσ’ ἄνδρεσσιν ἀνάσσων ‘being lord over Cilician men’, ἀνάσσω taking the dative.

sentences.t: τοῦ περ δὴ θυγάτηρ ἔχεθ’ Ἕκτορι χαλκοκορυστῇ.
sentences.l: Of him indeed the daughter was held by bronze-armed Hector.
sentences.i: It was his daughter that Hector, armed in bronze, had as his wife.
sentences.n: τοῦ περ δὴ ‘his indeed’ picks up Eetion. ἔχεθ’ (= ἔχετο) is the middle imperfect of ἔχω, ‘was held’, and with the dative Ἕκτορι it means she was held by Hector, that is, was his wife. The construction is unusual (the middle of ἔχω normally means ‘hold on to’, with the genitive), and ‘was his wife’ is the sense the context gives. χαλκοκορυστῇ ‘armed in bronze’ is Hector’s epithet here (κορύσσω ‘arm’).

sentences.t:
ἥ οἱ ἔπειτ’ ἤντησ’, ἅμα δ’ ἀμφίπολος κίεν αὐτῇ
παῖδ’ ἐπὶ κόλπῳ ἔχουσ’ ἀταλάφρονα νήπιον αὔτως
Ἑκτορίδην ἀγαπητὸν ἀλίγκιον ἀστέρι καλῷ,
sentences.l:
She then met him, and together a handmaid went with her
holding at her bosom the child, tender-minded, an infant simply,
Hector’s-son, beloved, like to a fair star,
sentences.i: She met him then, and with her went a handmaid holding to her bosom the little child, tender-minded, a mere infant, the beloved son of Hector, like a fair star,
sentences.n: A handmaid carries the baby with her. ἥ οἱ ἔπειτ’ ἤντησ’ ‘she then met him’: ἤντησε is the aorist of ἀντάω ‘meet’, and οἱ is ‘to him’. ἅμα … κίεν αὐτῇ ‘along with her went’ (κίεν is the unaugmented imperfect of κίω). ἀμφίπολος ‘handmaid’ holds the child ἐπὶ κόλπῳ ‘at her bosom’. ἀταλάφρονα ‘tender-minded’ is a rare compound (ἀταλός ‘tender’ + φρήν ‘mind’), and νήπιον αὔτως ‘an infant, simply’ means a mere baby. Ἑκτορίδην is a patronymic, ‘Hector’s-son’; ἀγαπητόν ‘beloved’; ἀλίγκιον ‘like’, with ἀστέρι καλῷ ‘a fair star’ in the dative.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ Ἕκτωρ καλέεσκε Σκαμάνδριον, αὐτὰρ οἱ ἄλλοι
Ἀστυάνακτ’·
sentences.l:
whom Hector kept calling Scamandrius, but the others
Astyanax;
sentences.i: whom Hector used to call Scamandrius, but the others called Astyanax;
sentences.n: The child has two names. τόν ῥ’ ‘whom indeed’ (the article used as a relative) takes up παῖδα; καλέεσκε is an iterative, with the ending -εσκ- showing a repeated action, ‘used to call’. αὐτὰρ οἱ ἄλλοι Ἀστυάνακτ’ ‘but the others Astyanax’: the verb ‘called’ is carried over from the first half. Σκαμάνδριον is formed on the river Scamander, and Ἀστυάναξ means ‘lord of the city’ (ἄστυ ‘town’ + ἄναξ ‘lord’).

sentences.t: οἶος γὰρ ἐρύετο Ἴλιον Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.l: for alone was guarding Ilios Hector.
sentences.i: for Hector alone guarded Ilios.
sentences.n: This gives the reason for the name Astyanax. οἶος γάρ ‘for alone’; ἐρύετο is the imperfect of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, protect’, so ‘was guarding’; Ἴλιον is ‘Ilios’. The child is called ‘lord of the city’ for what his father does.

sentences.t: ἤτοι ὃ μὲν μείδησεν ἰδὼν ἐς παῖδα σιωπῇ·
sentences.l: He indeed smiled, looking at the child, silent;
sentences.i: He, for his part, smiled silently as he looked at the child;
sentences.n: Hector’s reaction, set against Andromache’s in the next line. ἤτοι (one word in the edition) ‘indeed’ and ὃ μέν ‘he for his part’ look forward to Ἀνδρομάχη δέ ‘but Andromache’. μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω ‘smile’, ἰδὼν ἐς παῖδα ‘looking at the child’, and σιωπῇ ‘silent, in silence’ is a dative of manner.

sentences.t:
Ἀνδρομάχη δέ οἱ ἄγχι παρίστατο δάκρυ χέουσα,
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρὶ ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l:
And Andromache stood close beside him, a tear shedding,
and she clasped him by the hand, and spoke a word, and called him by name:
sentences.i: Andromache stood close beside him, shedding tears; she took his hand, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: Andromache comes close and takes his hand. Ἀνδρομάχη δέ ‘but Andromache’ answers Hector’s silence; παρίστατο ‘stood beside’ is the imperfect of παρίσταμαι, with οἱ ‘him’ and ἄγχι ‘near’; δάκρυ χέουσα ‘shedding a tear’. ἔν … φῦ is one verb split in two (= ἔμφυ), the aorist of ἐμφύω, ‘clung to’, with χειρί ‘by the hand’. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε ‘spoke a word and called him by name’ is a stock line for a gesture followed by speech.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνιε φθίσει σε τὸ σὸν μένος, οὐδ’ ἐλεαίρεις
παῖδά τε νηπίαχον καὶ ἔμ’ ἄμμορον, ἣ τάχα χήρη
σεῦ ἔσομαι·
sentences.i: “Strange man, your might will destroy you, and you have no pity on your little child, or on me, ill-fated as I am, who will soon be a widow bereft of you;
sentences.n: Andromache begins with a reproach: his own courage will kill him. δαιμόνιε ‘strange man’ is an address whose force is uncertain, ‘strange one, driven by something beyond himself’. φθίσει is the future of φθίω ‘waste, destroy’ used with an object, and τὸ σὸν μένος is ‘your might’. οὐδ’ ἐλεαίρεις ‘and you do not pity’; νηπίαχον ‘childish’ is built on νήπιος and is said of the baby, so the Greek says child twice. ἄμμορον ‘ill-fated’ is ἀ- ‘without’ + μόρος ‘portion’. τάχα ‘soon’; χήρη σεῦ ‘widow of you’, with σεῦ the genitive of what is lost.

sentences.t:
τάχα γάρ σε κατακτανέουσιν Ἀχαιοὶ
πάντες ἐφορμηθέντες·
sentences.l:
for soon will kill you the Achaeans,
all of them, having rushed upon you;
sentences.i: for soon the Achaeans will kill you, all of them rushing upon you;
sentences.n: The reason for her fear. τάχα γάρ ‘for soon’; κατακτανέουσιν is the future of κατακτείνω ‘kill’ in its uncontracted epic form; ἐφορμηθέντες is the aorist passive participle of ἐφορμάω ‘rush upon’, used like a middle, and πάντες ‘all’ agrees with Ἀχαιοί.

sentences.t:
ἐμοὶ δέ κε κέρδιον εἴη
σεῦ ἀφαμαρτούσῃ χθόνα δύμεναι·
sentences.l:
and for me it would be better,
having lost you, to go down into the earth;
sentences.i: and it would be better for me, once I have lost you, to go down into the earth;
sentences.n: She says she would rather die. ἐμοὶ δέ κε κέρδιον εἴη ‘and for me it would be better’ (κε with the optative); σεῦ ἀφαμαρτούσῃ ‘having lost you’ is a feminine dative participle agreeing with ἐμοί, and takes the genitive σεῦ. χθόνα δύμεναι ‘to go down into the earth’, δύμεναι being the infinitive of δύω; it means to die and be buried.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἄλλη
ἔσται θαλπωρὴ ἐπεὶ ἂν σύ γε πότμον ἐπίσπῃς
ἀλλ’ ἄχε’·
sentences.i: for I shall have no other comfort any more once you have met your doom, but only griefs;
sentences.n: Why she would rather die: nothing will be left to her. οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ ἄλλη … θαλπωρή ‘for no other comfort any more’ (θαλπωρή is ‘comfort’, related to θάλπω ‘warm’). ἐπεὶ ἂν … ἐπίσπῃς ‘when you shall have met’ is an aorist subjunctive of ἐφέπω, with πότμον ‘doom’. ἀλλ’ ἄχε’ ‘but griefs’: ἄχεα is the plural of ἄχος ‘grief’, and the verb ‘will be’ is carried over.

sentences.t: οὐδέ μοι ἔστι πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ.
sentences.l: nor have I a father and a lady mother.
sentences.i: I have neither father nor lady mother.
sentences.n: οὐδέ μοι ἔστι ‘nor is there to me’, with the nominatives πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ ‘father and lady mother’; πότνια ‘lady’ is a title of respect. She goes on to say how she lost them.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι γὰρ πατέρ’ ἁμὸν ἀπέκτανε δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἐκ δὲ πόλιν πέρσεν Κιλίκων εὖ ναιετάουσαν
Θήβην ὑψίπυλον·
sentences.i: For heavenly Achilles killed my father, and sacked the well-inhabited city of the Cilicians, high-gated Thebe;
sentences.n: Her family’s history begins with Achilles. ἤτοι γάρ ‘for indeed’ (ἤτοι is one word in the edition); ἁμόν is ‘my’, an epic form for ἐμόν; ἀπέκτανε ‘killed’, with πατέρ’ ἁμόν ‘my father’ as its object and δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς as its subject (the literal English keeps that order). ἐκ … πέρσεν is one verb split in two (= ἐξέπερσεν) ‘sacked’, with πόλιν ‘city’ and Θήβην in apposition. Κιλίκων is ‘of the Cilicians’, εὖ ναιετάουσαν ‘well-inhabited’, ὑψίπυλον ‘high-gated’. δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘heavenly Achilles’ is the stock epithet and name.

sentences.t:
κατὰ δ’ ἔκτανεν Ἠετίωνα,
οὐδέ μιν ἐξενάριξε, σεβάσσατο γὰρ τό γε θυμῷ,
ἀλλ’ ἄρα μιν κατέκηε σὺν ἔντεσι δαιδαλέοισιν
ἠδ’ ἐπὶ σῆμ’ ἔχεεν·
sentences.l:
and killed Eetion,
yet did not despoil him, for he felt awe at this in his heart,
but burned him with his wrought gear
and poured a tomb over him;
sentences.i: and he killed Eetion, but did not strip him of his armour, for he felt awe at this in his heart; he burned him with his finely wrought gear and heaped a tomb over him;
sentences.n: Achilles killed Eetion but gave him honourable burial. κατὰ … ἔκτανεν is one verb split in two (= κατέκτανεν) ‘killed’. οὐδέ μιν ἐξενάριξε ‘and he did not strip him’: ἐξεναρίζω is ‘kill and strip of armour’, here only the stripping. σεβάσσατο ‘felt awe’; τό γε ‘this at least’. κατέκηε ‘burned’ (= κατέκαιε); ἔντεσι δαιδαλέοισιν is ‘wrought gear’, that is, armour; ἐπὶ … ἔχεεν ‘poured on’, with σῆμα ‘tomb’, a mound.

sentences.t:
περὶ δὲ πτελέας ἐφύτευσαν
νύμφαι ὀρεστιάδες κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.l:
and around it planted elms
nymphs of the mountains, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.i: and around it the mountain nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, planted elms.
sentences.n: The nymphs honour the tomb. περὶ δὲ … ἐφύτευσαν ‘and around … planted’ (aorist of φυτεύω), with πτελέας ‘elms’ as object and the subject νύμφαι ὀρεστιάδες ‘nymphs of the mountains’ placed after. κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο ‘daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus’; αἰγιόχοιο is a stock epithet of Zeus whose sense is disputed.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ μοι ἑπτὰ κασίγνητοι ἔσαν ἐν μεγάροισιν
οἳ μὲν πάντες ἰῷ κίον ἤματι Ἄϊδος εἴσω·
sentences.l:
And I had seven brothers in the halls,
and they all went on one day into Hades;
sentences.i: I had seven brothers in our halls, and all of them went down to the house of Hades on a single day;
sentences.n: Her brothers. οἳ δέ μοι ἑπτὰ κασίγνητοι ἔσαν ‘and I had seven brothers’: οἳ is the article as a pronoun, μοι ‘to me’, ἔσαν = ἦσαν. οἳ μὲν πάντες ‘they, all of them’ takes the brothers up again. ἰῷ is an epic form meaning ‘one’; κίον is the unaugmented past of κίω ‘go’; Ἄϊδος εἴσω is ‘within Hades’, the house being left unsaid.

sentences.t:
πάντας γὰρ κατέπεφνε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
βουσὶν ἐπ’ εἰλιπόδεσσι καὶ ἀργεννῇς ὀΐεσσι.
sentences.l:
for all of them swift-footed, heavenly Achilles killed
at the rolling-gaited cattle and white sheep.
sentences.i: for swift-footed, heavenly Achilles killed them all among their cattle of rolling gait and their white sheep.
sentences.n: Achilles killed the brothers, again by himself. πάντας γάρ ‘for all of them’ (the object; Achilles is the subject); κατέπεφνε ‘killed’ (an old aorist with κατά). ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’: ποδάρκης is probably πούς ‘foot’ + ἀρκέω ‘ward off’, but the formation is not certain. βουσὶν ἐπ’ εἰλιπόδεσσι καὶ ἀργεννῇς ὀΐεσσι puts ἐπί + dative, ‘at’ the cattle and sheep, so they were with the herds; εἰλίπους is ‘rolling-gaited’ and ἀργεννός ‘white’.

sentences.t:
μητέρα δ’, ἣ βασίλευεν ὑπὸ Πλάκῳ ὑληέσσῃ,
τὴν ἐπεὶ ἂρ δεῦρ’ ἤγαγ’ ἅμ’ ἄλλοισι κτεάτεσσιν,
ἂψ ὅ γε τὴν ἀπέλυσε λαβὼν ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα,
πατρὸς δ’ ἐν μεγάροισι βάλ’ Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα.
sentences.l:
And my mother, who was queen beneath wooded Placus,
her, when he brought her here with the other possessions,
back he released her, having taken unstinted ransom,
but in her father’s halls Artemis, the arrow-pourer, hit her.
sentences.i: As for my mother, who was queen beneath wooded Placus: when he brought her here with the other possessions, he set her free again for an unstinted ransom, but in her father’s halls Artemis, who showers her arrows, hit her.
sentences.n: Her mother was ransomed and then died. μητέρα … τὴν: the accusative stands first and is taken up by τὴν ‘her’. βασίλευεν ‘was queen’; ἅμ’ ἄλλοισι κτεάτεσσιν ‘with the other possessions’; ἂψ … ἀπέλυσε ‘released again’; ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα ‘unstinted ransom’. πατρὸς is ‘her father’s’, her mother’s father. βάλ’ ‘hit’ is said of an arrow; the Greek gives no object, and the sense is that Artemis killed her. Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα ‘Artemis the arrow-pourer’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἀτὰρ σύ μοί ἐσσι πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
ἠδὲ κασίγνητος, σὺ δέ μοι θαλερὸς παρακοίτης·
sentences.l:
Hector, but you are to me father and lady mother
and brother, and you, to me, a flourishing consort;
sentences.i: Hector, but you are father to me, and lady mother, and brother, and you are my flourishing husband;
sentences.n: She sums up: Hector is everything to her. Ἕκτορ ἀτάρ ‘Hector, but’; σύ μοί ἐσσι ‘you are to me’, with the three nouns πατήρ ‘father’, μήτηρ ‘mother’ (πότνια ‘lady’) and κασίγνητος ‘brother’. θαλερός ‘flourishing’ and παρακοίτης, the masculine of παράκοιτις ‘consort’, one who shares the bed.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἐλέαιρε καὶ αὐτοῦ μίμν’ ἐπὶ πύργῳ,
μὴ παῖδ’ ὀρφανικὸν θήῃς χήρην τε γυναῖκα·
sentences.l:
But come now, have pity, and right here stay on the tower,
lest you make the child an orphan and a woman a widow;
sentences.i: But come now, have pity, and stay right here on the tower, so that you do not make your son an orphan and your wife a widow;
sentences.n: Her plea. ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ‘but come now’; ἐλέαιρε ‘pity’ (imperative; no object is given); αὐτοῦ ‘right here’; μίμν’ is μίμνε, the imperative of μίμνω ‘stay’, with ἐπὶ πύργῳ ‘on the tower’. μὴ … θήῃς is ‘lest you make’ (aorist subjunctive of τίθημι), with two objects and their complements: παῖδ’ ὀρφανικόν ‘the child an orphan’ and χήρην τε γυναῖκα ‘a woman a widow’.

sentences.t:
λαὸν δὲ στῆσον παρ’ ἐρινεόν, ἔνθα μάλιστα
ἀμβατός ἐστι πόλις καὶ ἐπίδρομον ἔπλετο τεῖχος.
sentences.l:
And station the people by the wild fig-tree, where above all
the city is scalable and the wall has proved open to assault.
sentences.i: And station the troops by the wild fig-tree, where the city can best be scaled and the wall is open to assault.
sentences.n: She advises where to place the army. λαὸν δέ ‘and the people’, that is the troops; στῆσον is the aorist imperative of ἵστημι, ‘station’. ἐρινεός is the wild fig-tree. ἔνθα μάλιστα ‘where most of all’; ἀμβατός ‘can be climbed’; ἐπίδρομον ‘one can run up to it’, so open to assault; ἔπλετο is an aorist that says what has proved true.

sentences.t:
τρὶς γὰρ τῇ γ’ ἐλθόντες ἐπειρήσανθ’ οἱ ἄριστοι
ἀμφ’ Αἴαντε δύω καὶ ἀγακλυτὸν Ἰδομενῆα
ἠδ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀτρεΐδας καὶ Τυδέος ἄλκιμον υἱόν·
sentences.i: For three times the best men have come to that spot and made trial of the wall, gathered around the two Ajaxes and renowned Idomeneus and around the sons of Atreus and the valiant son of Tydeus;
sentences.n: She says why that spot: the best men have tried it three times. τρὶς γάρ ‘for three times’; τῇ γ’ ‘at that place’; ἐλθόντες ἐπειρήσανθ’ ‘came and made trial’, ἐπειρήσανθ’ being ἐπειρήσαντο, from πειράομαι; the Greek gives no object, and ‘of the wall’ is supplied. οἱ ἄριστοι ‘the best men’ are named by their leaders with ἀμφί and the accusative, ‘around’: Αἴαντε δύω ‘the two Ajaxes’ (a dual), ἀγακλυτὸν Ἰδομενῆα ‘renowned Idomeneus’, Ἀτρεΐδας ‘the sons of Atreus’ (Agamemnon and Menelaus), and Τυδέος ἄλκιμον υἱόν ‘the valiant son of Tydeus’, named only by his father.

sentences.t:
ἤ πού τίς σφιν ἔνισπε θεοπροπίων ἐῢ εἰδώς,
ἤ νυ καὶ αὐτῶν θυμὸς ἐποτρύνει καὶ ἀνώγει.
sentences.l:
Either doubtless someone told them, well knowing the prophecies,
or indeed their own heart urges them on and bids them.”
sentences.i: Either some man who knew the prophecies well has doubtless told them, or their own heart urges them on and bids them.”
sentences.n: She guesses why they chose that spot. ἤ … ἤ ‘either … or’; πού ‘doubtless’ softens the guess. τίς σφιν ἔνισπε ‘someone told them’ (ἔνισπε is the unaugmented aorist of ἐνέπω ‘tell’); θεοπροπίων ἐῢ εἰδώς ‘knowing the prophecies well’, with θεοπρόπιον ‘prophecy’ in the genitive after εἰδώς. ἤ νυ καὶ ‘or indeed’; αὐτῶν θυμός ‘their own heart’; ἐποτρύνει … ἀνώγει ‘urges on and bids’. Her speech ends here.
